g.title: cluster_fk
g.text: FK TARGETING — the point of the hierarchy

g.title: fk
g.text: REAL FOREIGN KEYS → a subtype (possible only because each
child declares its own PRIMARY KEY — see the box below):
The FK target IS the business rule, enforced by the RDBMS:
a teacher cannot be enrolled; an admin cannot own a circle.
NO FK possible → app.users (polymorphic: any role):

g.title: n1
g.text: d = DISJOINT: a user is exactly one subtype.
Rows live in exactly ONE child. The parent is a read
surface: FROM app.users scans the whole hierarchy,
FROM ONLY app.users returns nothing. tableoid::regclass

g.title: n2
g.text: Postgres inherits columns, DEFAULTs, NOT NULL and CHECK.
It does NOT inherit these four — each is restored by hand:
IDENTITY → CREATE SEQUENCE app.user_id_seq, then a plain
(GENERATED AS IDENTITY yields NULL in children,
failing NOT NULL — no user could be created.)
One sequence keeps user_id unique across subtypes.
PRIMARY KEY → ALTER TABLE <child> ADD PRIMARY KEY (user_id).
Without it NO FK may reference a subtype at all.
UNIQUE → ADD UNIQUE (email) per child + assert_email_unique()
trigger; per-table UNIQUE cannot stop one address
existing as both a student and a teacher.
FK to parent → assert_user_exists() trigger. An FK to app.users
is checked with ONLY semantics: it sees no child
rows and would reject every real user.
